description.summary: The Fox Sister is a figure of Korean folklore in which a kumiho (nine-tailed fox spirit) takes the form of a young girl and infiltrates a family as their long-lost daughter, secretly devouring livestock and family members until exposed by an older brother.
description.full: The Fox Sister (여우 누이, yeowoo nui) is the title and central figure of one of the most widely circulated Korean folktales of the kumiho (구미호; Hanja 九尾狐, 'nine-tailed fox') tradition. In the canonical tale, recorded in late-19th and early-20th-century Korean folktale collections, an aging couple desperate for a daughter prays to the mountain spirit and is granted one — in fact, a kumiho in human form. The girl appears as a beautiful younger sister to the family's existing sons. After her arrival the family's livestock begin to die, one each night, with their livers torn out. The eldest sons are sent in turn to keep watch, fail (or are themselves killed), and only the youngest son (or, in some versions, an exiled elder brother) discovers the truth. Returning home with three magical bottles or talismans (often blue, red and white) given to him by a Buddhist monk or Daoist sage, he confronts his transformed 'sister' and destroys her. The Fox Sister fits within the wider East Asian fox-spirit complex (Chinese huli jing 狐狸精, Japanese kitsune 狐) but is distinctive in its Korean variant for the family-infiltration motif and the consistently malevolent characterisation of the kumiho. The term kumiho first appears in Korean writing in the poetry of Yi Kyubo (1168–1241) of the Goryeo dynasty; the medical compendium Donguibogam (compiled by Heo Jun, 1610) records a treatment for ailments attributed to the nine-tailed fox. The tale itself was widely collected during the Joseon and modern periods and provides the foundation for the post-1979 kumiho horror tradition in Korean television (notably KBS's Hometown of Legends / Jeonseol-ui Gohyang).

etymology.origin: Korean kumiho / gumiho (구미호) is a Sino-Korean compound from Hanja 九尾狐 (nine-tailed fox), parallel to Chinese jiuweihu and Japanese kyūbi no kitsune. 'Yeowoo nui' (여우 누이) is the native-Korean phrase 'fox sister' used as the folktale title.
etymology.meaning: Literally 'nine-tailed fox' (kumiho) or 'fox elder/younger sister' (yeowoo nui).
etymology.first_use: Term kumiho attested in Korean writing by Yi Kyubo (1168–1241); folktale 'Yeowoo Nui' widely collected in late-19th- and early-20th-century Korean folklore collections.

features.description: Default human form, used to gain entry to a household as a 'sister' or daughter
True form is a fox with nine tails; tails accumulate over centuries of cultivation
Premodern Korean sources describe foxes as white-furred; folktale illustrations often depict red-furred kumiho
Some kumiho carry a magical bead or 'fox marble' that is the source of their power; transferred between mouths during a kiss

physical.morphology: A nine-tailed vulpine in true form, capable of indistinguishable human disguise. Folkloric depictions emphasise the impossibility of detecting a kumiho on sight.

abilities.description: Takes the form of a beautiful woman or girl, sometimes after living 1,000 years (some folktale versions) or via the fox marble
Inserts herself into a household as an apparent daughter/sister
Drains gi (기) or eats the liver of livestock and humans, a key motif in the Fox Sister tale
Can produce illusions, conceal her tails, and bewitch men into compliance

behavior.diet: In the Fox Sister tale specifically: livers of livestock and humans, eaten one per night.
patterns: Appears at moments of family longing (childlessness, death of a daughter)
Uses kinship and hospitality as the route into the household
Defeated only by ritual / Buddhist–Daoist intervention (three colored bottles, talismans)

range.description: Korean folktale tradition (Korean peninsula and the wider Korean diaspora). The kumiho is part of the East Asian fox-spirit complex but the specific 'fox sister' motif is distinctively Korean.
countries: Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea)

origins.cultural_roots: The kumiho belongs to the wider East Asian fox-spirit complex, present in Chinese sources from the Han dynasty onwards. In the Korean version it absorbs strongly Buddhist and Daoist motifs (the three colored bottles, the role of the wandering monk) and a distinctive emphasis on family infiltration.
origins.earliest_accounts: The Samguk Sagi (1145) and Samgungnyusa (c. 1281) preserve early Korean fox-spirit references. The term kumiho (구미호) first appears in Korean literary writing in the poetry of Yi Kyubo (1168–1241).
origins.folklore_connections: Closely related to Chinese huli jing and Japanese kitsune; medieval Korean accounts also conflate the kumiho with mountain deities and shamanic figures.

timeline.event: Goryeo-era poet Yi Kyubo (1168–1241) uses the term kumiho in critical poetry comparing shamans to nine-tailed foxes
timeline.significance: Earliest dateable Korean attestation of the term

timeline.event: Heo Jun publishes the Donguibogam (Treasured Mirror of Eastern Medicine), which lists Byeogsadan as a treatment for illnesses caused by nine-tailed fox spirits
timeline.significance: Documented inclusion of kumiho-related ailments in formal Korean medicine

timeline.event: Joseon-era and early-modern folktale collections record multiple variants of 'Yeowoo Nui' (Fox Sister)
timeline.source: Various Korean folktale collections, late 19th – early 20th c.

timeline.event: Actress Han Hye-suk first portrays a kumiho in KBS's Hometown of Legends (Jeonseol-ui Gohyang)
timeline.significance: Beginning of the modern televised kumiho tradition

timeline.event: MBC drama My Girlfriend is a Gumiho premieres
timeline.significance: Major modern romantic-comedy reframing of the kumiho

timeline.event: tvN drama Tale of the Nine-Tailed (Gumiho-Jeon) premieres, with Lee Dong-wook in the lead role
timeline.significance: Major contemporary fantasy reception of the kumiho mythology

history.modern_era: The Fox Sister motif persists primarily within the wider kumiho tradition. Contemporary Korean television, film, manhwa, and games have reframed the kumiho across genres — horror (Hometown of Legends), romance (My Girlfriend is a Gumiho), and high-fantasy (Tale of the Nine-Tailed) — while the original Fox Sister folktale remains a staple of Korean children's folklore anthologies.

documentary.description: Heo Jun's compendium of Korean medicine, including a treatment formula (Byeogsadan) for ailments attributed to nine-tailed fox spirits.
documentary.analysis: Demonstrates the institutional recognition of kumiho-related belief in Joseon-era Korean medicine.

paranormal.name: Animistic / shamanic spirit
paranormal.description: Within Korean folk and shamanic tradition the kumiho is a real spirit-being with the capacity to inhabit the human world and harm households.
evidence_cited: Inclusion in the Donguibogam medical canon

scientific.name: Cultural-anxiety encoding
scientific.description: Folklorists read the Fox Sister as a cultural narrative encoding anxieties about family integrity, female sexuality, and the vulnerability of the domestic sphere to external threat under Confucian patriarchal social structures.
evidence_cited: Comparative analysis with Chinese and Japanese fox traditions
Pattern of female-coded fox spirits in Joseon-era texts

folklore.beliefs: Within Korean folk belief the kumiho is consistently depicted as malevolent, in marked contrast to the more ambiguous Chinese huli jing and the often benevolent Japanese kitsune. The 'fox sister' subtype emphasises the specific danger of strangers introduced into the household under the guise of kinship.
